b: The "debut album" by the Preston-born musician, rapper and choreographer establishes Blackhaine as one of the most confident voices in the new Northern Gothic scene developing around Yorkshire and Lancashire

In the film, The King (2019), we see a stubborn Dauphin of France attempting to end the Battle of Agincourt through a duel with King Henry. Heavy rainfall has left the ground entirely sodden, and before a single blow is dealt, the Dauphin is slipping and sliding around the squelchy ground, falling over and over again. He is tragically defenceless and vulnerable as he performs an unchoreographed, increasingly desperate dance of misery before being swiftly slaughtered and left dead in the mud.

This painful scene is soundtracked by Nicolas Britell’s fabulously somber ‘Hymn – Mvmt 2’ and the same score is appropriately woven into the fabric of ‘Spirit’, taken from the debut album by Lancashire musician and choreographer Blackhaine (aka Tom Heyes). The track tussles with Heyes’ own mortality, alluding to two previous occasions he nearly lost his life, which in turn leaves the listener emotionally contemplating their own mortality. Throughout ‘Spirit’ – and Heyes’ album Saints in The Wethouse more generally – runs the idea of finding different languages beyond words to express how battering and disconnected life can feel.

In live performance, Heyes can be seen using the body as a vessel to exorcise and cleanse a life of self-annihilation and gluttony, as if throwing cold water onto his face to wake himself up. Heyes’ own dance form draws on the Japanese style of butoh, a post-World War II anti-establishment movement set against both Western and Japanese traditions. In an interview with the Quietus’ Alastair Shuttleworth in 2022, Heyes talked about his experience feeling disenfranchised from the UK dancing scene: “I just got angry with it and decided to do my own thing.” Musically, this non-conformism oozes out of Saints in The Wethouse from the very first track. On ‘Cold Shoulder’, Heyes rails: “try to sue me for shit, I shouldn’t talk back” against cutthroat synths and sparse, marching percussion.

Excitingly, the industrial sound of the record never lets up, and makes the album a timely Northern Gothic successor to Kanye West’s groundbreaking Yeezus (2013). Take ‘Consumer’, which features emotive vocals from Jamaican dancehall artist Mad Cobra following a panicked malfunction of siren-sounding synths. The combination is not dissimilar to West’s ‘I’m In It’, which featured Assassin, another Jamaican dancehall artist. Both tracks incite a burning indignation that builds in a frankly thrilling way, in Blackhaine’s case prompted by an example of uncompromising sonic jolts that pop up throughout the album, giving your ears no respite.

Similarly, on ‘Northside Needs Me’, Heyes raps about drug-fuelled benders and sex sessions against a backdrop of what the lyrics identify as “Northside rain”. Once again, the track has a raging instrumental, this time akin to West’s ‘On Sight’, all soulful chops and grandiose synth stabs (West’s track also soundtracked a viral video of West and Heyes dancing on stage together in China in 2024).

Heyes’ northern working class setting, where bravado masks a helpless lack of agency is woven deep into both the record’s lyrics and sound. ‘5 Days’ begins with a clip of a protester talking about the 2011 Salford riots, maintaining that people “are seen as scum, so they act like scum,” before Heyes paints a familiar Northern England picture of staring “out the window, everything grey” as the industrial instrumental comprises a congregation of echoes darting around sawing synths, like an abandoned factory’s ghosts trying to escape its brick walls.

Nonetheless, through this new album we also hear for the first time Heyes yearning to escape the grinding reality of his rockstar life as he is living it, in hope of accessing something more grounded, less slippery. The first seeds of this aspiration are evident in ‘Pyrex’ although he remains fully alert to the challenge it poses. Heyes talks about driving up and down the A6 but remains clear that if his career doesn’t work out he will inevitably resort to drug dealing, even listing his preemptive tools like a shopping list: “G class, burner phone, deep grass, serpent roam”. It’s this yin and yang of Heyes’ braggadocious lyrics set against his own self-awareness that enriches the album so powerfully. For now, he is simply standing on his own, the mood feels bleak, but the propulsive percussion is still full of vigour and fight.

The final track, ‘Saints In The Wethouse’, starts with haunting moans floating around a windy ambience. Heyes crawls back to the wethouse to drink. He is drowning in his feelings and perceiving “silence as a persecution,” painfully torn between the need to control and shape experience and the deep fear of formlessness. This is played out through eight minutes of deteriorating sonic textures, as we go from Heyes’ scarily calm vocals into drones which then crescendo into an erupting soundscape you might hear from the likes of Klein.

This uncanny cacophony of noise is the auditory dramatisation of considerable internal suffering. You feel Heyes’ pain as his world collapses at the wethouse. It’s unsettling to listen to. This is a far cry from declaring on ‘Artwork’ that he has “turned [his] life to a high price artwork,” therein articulating a particularly modern day fear: a form of gothic horror where you can so easily lose everything only to end up cooking drugs in a Pyrex jug. It’s enough of a prospect to make you turn to religion.

So, “Is Salvation free?” Heyes duly asks on ‘Never Alone’, in a voice suggesting he is rather wary of such a prospect. How can salvation be affordable if you have lost everything? Although on ‘Born From Wounds [Floodlights]’, Heyes’ desperate screams once again break down into distorted noise, from this pit he considers “stepping in front of the train to see the floodlights,” in effect putting himself in harm’s way in order to be touched by the sublime. But he comes out the other side of the track with an angelic aura protecting his screams, moving towards a rare sense of peace on the record. On the next track, ‘The Wind’, a wonderful acoustic duet co-produced with Space Afrika, an air of calm and content has mercifully swept over Heyes, and he resists the sirens’ call to look back.

Rainy Miller and Heyes are bonded by their Preston roots, and are both protagonists of the Northern Gothic scene. It’s a movement that has flowered like a red Lancastrian rose out of a concrete pavement. Artists such as Miller, Heyes, Aya, Richie Culver and DJ DEATHDEFY combine harsh sonics and an experimental pizzazz with some Northern charm, while the subject matter characteristically circles around isolation and disenfranchisement. Heyes’ Saints In The Wethouse is a perfect example of the visceral emotional pull that the most stirring albums from these genres can create, accosting you with a constant juxtaposition of calm moments in the midst of a storm, and even, sometimes, beauty in the mundane.

If the acoustic nature of ‘The Wind’ functions as the cool breeze and landscape of the Kersal Wetlands, the rest of the album dramatises the landscape of Salford’s industrial past, with Space Afrika, Croww, Rainy Miller all contributing to the production of the record, while ‘Valium’ sounds like it could be a Ship Sket production with its maximalist melodies and skatty bass. However, the biggest contribution is Wraith9, who produces multiple tracks on the record (just listen for the “OK” tag). Known for his work with Esdeekid and Fakemink, the British producer here creates the perfect canvas for Heyes’ depth and vulnerability with his uncompromising beats.

On this form, one can only hope that the UK underground rap scene continues to be pushed in the direction Heyes is now probing. He’s moved past his previous drill sound into a more neo-gothic space fuelled by anti-establishment ire, albeit now tempered more by a growing self-awareness. In his previous interview with the Quietus, Heyes self-deprecatingly quoted Terry Malloy’s “I coulda been a contender” line from the end of On the Waterfront (1954) in response to previous lyrics from his early EPs, Armour and Armour II. But a contender he certainly is now, confidently making music with a striking clarity and honesty.
